thesis: This episode argues that Gucci was a prime acquisition target for LVMH due to its rapid growth under Tom Ford and its vulnerability to brand dilution from excessive licensing. It details how Bernard Arnault initially backed out of a deal but later regretted it, eventually acquiring a significant stake after Gucci implemented an employee stock ownership plan.

claims.claim: Gucci was a target for LVMH but Bernard Arnault backed out of a deal, later regretting it, before eventually acquiring a stake.
claims.quote: This was an obvious target for LVMH to scoop up. In fact, Bernard goes and talks to Investcorp and reaches a verbal agreement in the mid 90s to buy Gucci from them for $400 million.

claims.claim: Gucci's brand was diluting with too many licenses, making it hard to distinguish from counterfeits.
claims.quote: Gucci at this point had, I kid you not, 22,000 different licenses like toilet paper. Ben: You can see Gucci on the street and you'd have no idea if that was a counterfeit or if something of that quality was actually Gucci.

claims.claim: Gucci's revenue doubled overnight after Tom Ford's first collections, and the brand became very hot.
claims.quote: Overnight, after Tom Ford's first collections, Gucci revenue doubles. They get back to profitability. At the end of 1994, when Bernard walked away from the deal, by the end of 1995, the brand is so hot that Investcorp IPO is the company on the New York Stock Exchange, and it trades up to a $3 billion market cap.

claims.claim: Gucci was incorporated in the Netherlands, allowing them to create an ESOP with 25.5% of the company without alerting shareholders.
claims.quote: They issue it 25.5% of the company. LVMH is shocked because their understanding from having studied the files on this is that if you're traded on the New York Stock Exchange, you can't do a transaction for 20% or more of the company without alerting all shareholders and getting a special exemption.

claims.claim: Gucci's lawyer proposed creating an employee stock ownership plan (an ESOP) with 25% of the company as a last ditch attempt.
claims.quote: He's like, well, if nobody outside is going to buy a huge block of Gucci stock and save you from LVMH, what if we do it on the inside? We can create an employee stock ownership plan (an ESOP), and what if we just give the ESOP something like 25% of the company?

claims.claim: Gucci agreed that Francois Pinault would invest $3 billion at $75 a share for 42% of Gucci.
claims.quote: In the next few days, they agree that Pino is going to invest $3 billion at $75 a share for 42% of Gucci.
